title: Habakkuk 2:1–5
context: Habakkuk takes his stand like a watchman to see how the LORD will answer his complaint (2:1). The LORD tells him to write the vision plainly, because it awaits an appointed time and will surely come, even if it seems slow (2:2–3). At the heart of the answer stands a contrast: the one whose soul is “puffed up” is not upright, “but the righteous will live by his faith” (2:4). The Hebrew word behind “faith” can also mean faithfulness or steadfastness, and readers in both traditions weigh how much the line stresses trust, faithful endurance, or both. The New Testament uses the line three times, each in its own setting: Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 render it “by faith,” without “his,” in arguments about the righteousness of God and justification apart from the law, and Hebrews 10:38 speaks of “the righteous one” who lives by faith while awaiting the one who comes. For the classic Arminian and Reformed readings, see the Romans 1:17 box and the Hebrews 10:38 box; see also Galatians 3:11, which has no separate catalog entry. These notes do not add a parallel discussion. Verse 5 returns to the proud man, restless and insatiable as death. Shared ground: both traditions read 2:4 as contrasting pride with trust in God and treat the New Testament uses as distinct applications rather than merging them.

verses.text: I will stand at my watch and set myself on the ramparts, and will look out to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer concerning my complaint.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will stand at my watch and set myself on the ramparts.” Habakkuk takes the posture of a watchman waiting for the LORD’s reply. Arminian readers see active, expectant faith: the prophet positions himself to hear and is ready to answer “concerning my complaint.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet submitting his questions to God’s word, waiting for revelation rather than reasoning his way to an answer. Shared ground: both traditions read the watchtower as an image of patient, attentive waiting on God, whether the post was literal or figurative, and both see the honest complaint as offered to God for his answer.

verses.text: The LORD answered me, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers Habakkuk: “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it.” Arminian readers see God’s concern that the message be clear and widely accessible, so that people can hear it and respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the written, public character of revelation: what God declares is fixed and certain, recorded so that its fulfillment can be recognized. Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge that “he who runs may read it” may mean a herald running with the message or a reader taking it in at a glance, and both value plain, public revelation.

verses.text: For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it, because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the vision is yet for the appointed time.” Arminian readers hear a call to patient faith: “Though it takes time, wait for it.” Waiting is active trust in God’s faithfulness, not passive resignation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress “the appointed time”: God has fixed the moment of fulfillment, and “it will surely come,” however slow it seems from a human vantage. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as assurance that God’s word will be fulfilled in his time, and both note that Hebrews 10:37 draws on this language for the coming of Christ, a use named without merging.

verses.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.” Arminian readers contrast the proud with the righteous, who live by trusting God, and many stress that the Hebrew word can also mean faithfulness. They read Paul’s use as faith being the grace-enabled condition of receiving God’s favor (see the Romans 1:17 box).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as foundational for justification by faith alone, read through Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11, while affirming that true faith perseveres (see the Hebrews 10:38 box). Shared ground: both traditions read the line as contrasting pride with trust in God, acknowledge the faith-and-faithfulness question, and treat the New Testament uses as distinct.

verses.text: Yes, moreover, wine is treacherous: an arrogant man who doesn’t stay at home, who enlarges his desire as Sheol; he is like death and can’t be satisfied, but gathers to himself all nations and heaps to himself all peoples.
verses.arminianNotes: “Yes, moreover, wine is treacherous: an arrogant man who doesn’t stay at home.” Arminian readers see the arrogant conqueror as restless and insatiable, “like death and can’t be satisfied,” a picture of desire chosen and fed until it consumes nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boundless appetite of the proud, compared with Sheol, the place of the dead, as the opposite of the trust of the righteous in verse 4. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as continuing the portrait of the puffed-up soul, most likely Babylon’s ruler or the nation, and both see insatiable greed as the mark of a life not lived by faith.
